clinicalPearls: A defect of the atrioventricular septum with a common or shared atrioventricular junction, from failure of endocardial cushion development
Complete forms have a primum atrial septal defect, an inlet ventricular septal defect and a common atrioventricular valve
It is strongly associated with Down syndrome
Complete AVSD causes a large left-to-right shunt with heart failure and, if untreated, pulmonary vascular disease
A left-axis (superior) QRS axis on the electrocardiogram is characteristic
Surgical repair in infancy is required for complete defects to prevent irreversible pulmonary hypertension
reference.pathophysiology: Atrioventricular septal defect results from deficient development of the endocardial cushions, which normally form the lower atrial septum, the inlet ventricular septum and the septal components of the atrioventricular valves. The resulting defect allows shunting at atrial and/or ventricular level and produces a common or abnormal atrioventricular valve that is often regurgitant. A large left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow, causing heart failure in infancy and, if uncorrected, progressive pulmonary vascular remodelling toward irreversible pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology).
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of infantile heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography defining the defect and atrioventricular valve
Assessment for Down syndrome and other associations
Cardiac catheterisation or advanced imaging where pulmonary vascular resistance is in question
Monitoring for heart failure and pulmonary hypertension
redFlags: Signs of heart failure in infancy
Evidence of rising pulmonary vascular resistance
reference.prognosis: With timely surgical repair outcomes are generally good, though residual atrioventricular valve regurgitation and left ventricular outflow obstruction may need reintervention; delayed repair risks irreversible pulmonary vascular disease.
pitfalls: Delaying repair of a complete defect and allowing pulmonary vascular disease
Missing the diagnosis in a child with Down syndrome and subtle signs
Overlooking left ventricular outflow tract obstruction after repair
management: Undertake surgical repair in infancy for complete defects, patching the atrial and ventricular components and reconstructing the atrioventricular valves, to prevent irreversible pulmonary vascular disease
Manage heart failure medically before operation with diuretics, afterload reduction and high-calorie nutritional support to optimise growth
Assess for and manage the strongly associated Down syndrome and its comorbidities
Perform postoperative surveillance for residual atrioventricular valve regurgitation, left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and arrhythmia, any of which may require reintervention
Monitor for pulmonary hypertension and assess pulmonary vascular resistance when repair is delayed
Coordinate care through a congenital cardiology and cardiac surgical multidisciplinary team
